target.title: emg2speech: synthesizing speech from electromyography using self-supervised speech models

read.pdf: Figures 1–10 and Tables 1–6, including captions, plotted axes, and reference list

entries.text: The method translates orofacial EMG recorded during articulation directly into synthesized audio.
entries.condition: The system is demonstrated on a healthy participant and one participant with ALS; ALS speech is silently articulated.

entries.text: Training does not require known frame-level temporal alignment between EMG and audio; the target speech units are transcript-derived.
entries.condition: The paper derives HuBERT units from Google TTS audio synthesized from transcripts; this audio is not time-aligned with EMG.

entries.text: The synthesis targets come from transcript-based gTTS audio, not the participant's recorded audio; the latter is used only for linearity probing.
entries.condition: Applies to DATA GENERAL and DATA ALS; for the healthy participant, recorded audio is reserved for the preceding probe.
entries.quote: we do not use subject-recorded audio for EMG-to-speech synthesis.

entries.text: The authors claim the released corpora are among the largest and most comprehensive public EMG-to-speech resources to date, qualified as to their knowledge.
entries.condition: The claim concerns the healthy large-vocabulary corpus and the ALS small-vocabulary corpus together.

entries.text: DATA GENERAL contains approximately 9 hours of EMG speech and over 6,800 unique words from one healthy participant.
entries.condition: Healthy participant; large-vocabulary corpus. Sec. 3.1 separately reports 9,660 sentences, 115 words/minute, and an 8,500/760/400 train/validation/test split.
entries.quote:

entries.text: DATA ALS contains approximately 1 hour of EMG speech and roughly 300 unique words from one participant with ALS.
entries.condition: Single ALS participant; small-vocabulary corpus with silent articulation. Sec. 3.2 reports 600 sentences, 61 words/minute, and a 500/40/60 train/validation/test split.
entries.quote:

vocabulary corpus of approximately 1 hour of EMG

entries.text: The authors claim the encoder works in a low-data regime, including with 40 minutes of ALS-participant training data.
entries.condition: One ALS participant; the main ALS corpus has 500 training sentences, 40 validation sentences, and 60 test sentences.

entries.text: The authors claim, for the first time, to establish a quantitative relationship between EMG signals and self-supervised speech representations.
entries.condition: The probe maps speech representation H to per-channel EMG power D(E) using DATA GENERAL.

entries.text: A simple linear map predicts EMG power from self-supervised speech features with Pearson correlation r=0.85.
entries.condition: Train linear mapping on DATA GENERAL training split and evaluate on its 400-sentence test split; one healthy participant; H is extracted from recorded participant audio; models/layers include HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, and wavLM.

entries.text: Unsupervised k-medoids accuracy using diagonal EMG power D(E) is 61.41% averaged across 12 subjects.
entries.condition: DATA OROFACIAL GESTURES: 13 gesture classes; k-medoids on D(E); average across 12 healthy participants. The t-SNE illustration is from one subject.

entries.text: Using the full EMG covariance matrix with the stated geodesic distance raises k-medoids accuracy to 73.7%.
entries.condition: DATA OROFACIAL GESTURES: 13 gesture classes, trials from 12 healthy participants; full covariance E and geodesic distance; averaged subject-level result is not specified separately.

entries.text: The authors give 7.69% as random-chance accuracy for the 13-way gesture clustering evaluation.
entries.condition: DATA OROFACIAL GESTURES; 13 distinct movement labels; compared with k-medoids accuracies for D(E) and full covariance E.

entries.text: The maximum reported correlation between EMG spectrogram features and H is approximately 0.57.
entries.condition: Linear probe between H and five-bin EMG spectrogram features on DATA GENERAL; layer-wise results in Fig. 3; held-out test split is described for the preceding probe, but per-layer selection details are not given.

entries.text: The comparison linear mapping between audio spectrogram A and EMG power D(E) has correlation r=0.61.
entries.condition: DATA GENERAL linear mapping comparison; the paper says this is considerably lower than the H-to-D(E) correlation.

entries.text: The paper reports Gaddy and Klein (2020) at 68% WER on the large-vocabulary corpus.
entries.condition: Prior EMG-to-speech benchmark cited by the target paper; exact split, speaker/session setup, and decoding conditions are not restated here.

entries.text: The paper reports Gaddy and Klein (2021) at 42% WER on the large-vocabulary corpus.
entries.condition: Prior EMG-to-speech benchmark cited by the target paper; exact split, speaker/session setup, and decoding conditions are not restated here.

entries.text: Benster et al. (2024) report WER below 10% on the Gaddy and Klein (2020) dataset using an LLM to post-correct intermediate EMG-to-phoneme output.
entries.condition: Target paper says the method no longer supports streaming synthesis and its evaluation does not fully characterize potential LLM text leakage; conditions are not one-to-one comparable.

entries.text: Littlejohn et al. (2025) report 74% WER on the Gaddy and Klein (2020) dataset using a CNN+RNN transducer.
entries.condition: Target paper says train-test splits and implementation details are not publicly available, preventing direct comparison.

entries.text: Wairagkar et al. (2025) report median WER 43% using 256 intracortical electrodes, approximately 8,300 cued sentences, and about 38 hours of data.
entries.condition: Invasive cortical speech interface; comparison is contextual, not one-to-one with the unaligned EMG setting.

entries.text: Metzger et al. (2023) report WER 54% using 253 electrodes and a 1,024-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: Invasive motor-cortex interface; comparison is contextual, not one-to-one with the target paper's EMG condition.

entries.text: The paper says Littlejohn et al. use a 1,024-word small-vocabulary corpus and each test sentence was presented an average of 6.94 times during training.
entries.unit: vocabulary words; training presentations per test sentence on average
entries.condition: Prior motor-cortex-to-speech study; the target paper cites this to contrast data/split difficulty, not as a directly comparable score.

entries.text: The authors explicitly warn against one-to-one comparisons across studies because collection, targets, alignment assumptions, task formulation, and evaluation differ.
entries.condition: Applies to the contextual WER comparisons in Appendix C, including neural and EMG interfaces.

entries.text: The authors state there are no existing benchmarks supporting direct one-to-one comparison for transcript-derived, unaligned EMG-to-speech synthesis.
entries.condition: They provide representative baselines and broader context, explicitly not direct comparisons.

entries.text: The authors propose a non-invasive interface for people with preserved articulatory muscle activity, including people with laryngectomy, dysarthria, or dysphonia.
entries.condition: Proposed clinical potential; the study demonstrates one ALS participant and does not establish broad clinical effectiveness.

entries.text: Speech EMG is recorded at 5,000 Hz from 31 surface-electrode sites; the reference channel is subtracted, signals are 80–1,000 Hz filtered, segmented by timestamps, and z-normalized per channel over time.
entries.condition: DATA GENERAL and DATA ALS use the same electrode layout; ALS articulation is silent. Gesture dataset uses 22 electrodes instead.

entries.text: The gesture corpus has 12 healthy participants, 13 movement labels, 10 repetitions per movement, 22 electrodes, 5,000-Hz sampling, and 1.5-second trials.
entries.unit: participants; movements; repetitions; electrodes; Hz; seconds
entries.condition: DATA OROFACIAL GESTURES; right-side neck electrodes are omitted relative to DATA GENERAL.

entries.text: Sequences are emitted every 20 ms with a 25-ms context window; the causal TDS model has a 1-second causal receptive field.
entries.condition: Sequence-to-sequence model for speech features; causal convolutions and a shift-tolerant electrode-channel module.

entries.text: The principal synthesis decoder predicts 100 HuBERT-BASE units from layer 6 with CTC and greedy search; a pretrained Tacotron vocoder renders the predicted units to audio.
entries.condition: Unit targets are extracted from transcript-based gTTS audio; inference decodes only the unit head in the phoneme-guided model.

entries.text: The phoneme decoder predicts 40 English phonemes and uses greedy search; PER is normalized by target phoneme-sequence length.
entries.condition: CTC phoneme decoding on DATA GENERAL; decoding outputs are compared with transcript-derived target phoneme sequences.

entries.text: Phoneme-guided training adds a phoneme head, two CTC objectives, and a consistency loss; the appendix sets loss weights to 0.8, 0.1, and 0.1 for unit CTC, phoneme CTC, and consistency.
entries.condition: The phoneme-to-unit table is fixed during encoder training; inference decodes only the unit head.
entries.quote: In our experiments, we useλunit = 0.8,λphone = 0.1, andλ cons = 0.1.

entries.text: The paper specifies AdamW with learning rate 3×10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻⁴, 5 warm-up epochs, cosine decay to 10⁻⁶, and 50 training epochs with temporal-jitter resampling.
entries.unit: learning rate; weight decay; epochs; minimum learning rate; epochs
entries.condition: Appendix D.5 gives β1=0.9 and β2=0.98; model training uses train split, validation loss, and per-epoch temporal jitter resampling.

entries.text: The method generates audio without explicitly training a vocoder, while using a pretrained Tacotron vocoder at inference.
entries.condition: HuBERT units predicted from EMG are passed into the pretrained vocoder.

entries.text: The authors claim phoneme-guided decoding improves generated-audio quality because multi-site EMG captures phonetic structure more faithfully than HuBERT audio units.
entries.condition: Reported objective evidence is lower HuBERT-unit UER; human WER is reported for the phoneme-guided vec(E) synthesis.
entries.quote:
Third, we introduce phoneme-guided decoding
for EMG-to-speech synthesis and show that incor-
porating phonetic structure improves the quality of
the generated audio.

entries.text: The authors qualify the 3.79 MOS interpretation: acoustic plausibility can remain moderate despite high WER because the recovered linguistic representation is noisy and the vocoder was trained on natural speech.
entries.condition: MOS reflects perceived waveform plausibility, whereas WER reflects recovered linguistic-content fidelity.
entries.quote: why MOS remains moderately high despite high WER:

entries.text: The clinical demonstration uses approximately one hour of data from one ALS participant and does not characterize day-to-day EMG distribution shifts.
entries.condition: The paper names electrode placement, skin impedance, fatigue, and disease progression as potential sources of distribution shift.
entries.quote: Our clinical demonstration uses approximately one hour of data from a single participant with ALS.

entries.text: The authors do not demonstrate sustained long-term performance of the non-invasive neuroprosthesis.
entries.condition: Longitudinal robustness and deployment stability remain unmeasured in this study.
entries.quote:
In addition, we do not demonstrate sustained,
long-term performance of this non-invasive neuro-
prosthesis.

entries.text: The authors do not test whether large-scale pretrained EMG-to-speech models would improve decoding performance.
entries.condition: They cite multi-person pretraining for EMG keyboard typing as motivation, but do not evaluate such pretraining for speech.

entries.text: The paper does not state the number or identity of recording sessions, or whether train, validation, and test sentences are separated by session.
entries.condition: Applies to both speech corpora; sentence-level separation is stated, but session-level separation is not.
entries.quote: We split the dataset into training, validation, and test sets containing 8500, 760, and 400 sentences, respectively.

entries.text: The speech evaluations do not test held-out-speaker generalization: all DATA GENERAL splits come from one healthy participant and all DATA ALS splits from one ALS participant.
entries.condition: The paper provides sentence-disjoint train/validation/test splits, not participant-disjoint splits; gesture analysis separately uses 12 healthy participants.
entries.quote: A healthy participant naturally articulates English sentences while the corresponding EMG signals are recorded at 5000 Hz.

entries.text: For Tables 1–4, five random seeds are reported, but seed values, per-seed scores, and the meaning of ± (standard deviation, standard error, or another interval) are not stated.

entries.text: No speech-decoding chance level or random baseline is reported for UER, PER, WER, or MOS; the stated 7.69% chance level applies only to the 13-class gesture analysis.
entries.condition: Speech metrics use held-out DATA GENERAL/DATA ALS test sets; chance performance is not defined for MOS and is not supplied for sequence error rates.

entries.text: For k-medoids gesture accuracies, the paper does not state the train/test procedure, initialization, number of restarts, or how subject-level scores are aggregated for the full-covariance result.

questions.q: How does the paper train and run EMG-to-speech without aligned EMG-audio recordings?
questions.answer: It obtains HuBERT-unit targets from transcript-based gTTS audio, trains a causal TDS encoder with CTC (and, in the phoneme-guided version, an additional phoneme head and consistency loss), then greedily decodes units and renders them with a pretrained Tacotron vocoder.

questions.q: What are the principal quantitative outcomes and their evaluation conditions?
questions.answer: For DATA GENERAL, vec(E) has 56.08±0.91% UER and 32.78±0.66% PER on 400 held-out sentences, with five-seed averages; phoneme-guided unit decoding gives 51.81±0.62% UER. Human WER averages 62.55±2.40% on the healthy test set and 50.82±1.59% on the ALS test set; MOS is 3.79 from 350 ratings on a 35-sentence subset.

questions.q: Which code-only evaluation conditions should a reviewer track?
questions.answer: The General split is made by corpus-order slicing; the ALS test indices are randomly selected and remaining records are split by order; notebooks select the minimum-validation-loss checkpoint, do not set a fixed training seed, and evaluation applies Whisper English text normalization and g2p_en phonemization.

questions.q: What prevents broad deployment or generalization claims?
questions.answer: The clinical demonstration uses one ALS participant and about one hour of data; session-level separation, held-out-speaker performance, day-to-day robustness, and sustained long-term performance are not established, and the authors did not test large-scale EMG pretraining.

questions.q: How should the reported literature comparisons be interpreted?
questions.answer: As context rather than head-to-head evidence: the paper explicitly says collection setups, targets, alignment assumptions, task formulations, and evaluation methods differ; it also leaves the EMG2TEXT training/evaluation split unclear.

questions.q: Is the phoneme-guided gain measured by listeners, or only by unit error rate?
questions.answer: Only UER (Tables 3 and 4) compares unit-CTC-only against phoneme-guided training; human WER (Table 5) is reported only for the phoneme-guided vec(E) model.

questions.q: Did the healthy participant produce audio that could have served as the target?
questions.answer: Yes: the healthy participant vocalized (footnote 3), and the recorded audio is used only for the linearity probe; no own-audio target condition is reported.
